brief.headline: Lucas had an ED visit on 10/30 for a UTI with acute confusion, and he has lost 7.1% of his body weight since 9/5 (93.6 to 87.0 kg), so the team should review both.

items.statement: Lucas went to the partner hospital ED on 2026-10-30 for a urinary tract infection with acute confusion. He was treated and released the same day on nitrofurantoin 100 MG for 5 days (10/30 to 11/04). The PCP post-hospital visit on 11/05 was within the 7-day follow-up window.
items.verifier_note: The discharge summary and the encounter record both show the 10/30 ED visit for UTI with acute confusion, with same-day release. The nitrofurantoin 100 MG course for 5 days (10/30 to 11/04) matches the medication record. The 11/05 PCP visit is 6 days after 10/30, so it falls inside the 7-day follow-up window.

items.statement: On 11/03 Linda reported about two weeks of evening confusion, including once leaving the stove on. Lucas was oriented to person and place but not date, with no fever. The RN planned a urinalysis, medication review and PCP visit. On 11/05 the PCP noted he was back to baseline per his son and planned close monitoring for two weeks.
items.verifier_note: The 11/03 nursing note and the 11/05 PCP note match every detail in the statement.

items.statement: Weight fell from 93.6 kg (9/5) to 91.3 (10/1), 89.0 (10/28) and 87.0 kg (11/24). That is a 6.6 kg (14.6 lb), 7.1% loss. On 11/24 the dietitian documented poor appetite, skipped breakfasts and about 50% of day center lunches eaten. The plan is an oral nutrition supplement twice daily, weekly weights and a dental check for chewing problems.
items.verifier_note: The four weights, the 6.6 kg, 14.6 lb and 7.1% change, and the dietitian's findings and plan all match the vitals record and the 11/24 note.

items.statement: Linda raised the evening confusion and the stove incident on 11/03, and Lucas's son reported he was back to baseline on 11/05. The notes do not document any home safety plan after the stove incident.
items.verifier_note: The stove incident on 11/03 and the son's report of baseline on 11/05 are documented. Neither cited note contains a home safety plan, so the absence statement holds for these notes.

items.statement: The only medication change in the period was the nitrofurantoin short course (10/30 to 11/04). The 11/03 medication review was planned, but its outcome is not documented in the notes provided.
items.verifier_note: The medication record shows only the nitrofurantoin course, and nothing was stopped. The 11/03 note plans a medication review. The notes give no outcome of that review, only a 11/05 review of discharge medications.

questions_for_team: Were the urinalysis and medication review planned on 11/03 completed, and what did they show?
Was the two-week monitoring period set by the PCP on 11/05 completed, and has the evening confusion recurred?
Does the team need a home safety plan for stove use, given the 11/03 report?
Is the weight loss being reviewed alongside the recent infection and confusion? Who owns the weekly weights and the dental referral?
How will the team follow intake at the day center and at home, given about 50% of lunches eaten and skipped breakfasts?

checks: Confirm the review window (2026-09-01 to 2026-11-30) and that the enrollment-to-review interval is correctly used; note the last IDT review date if one exists, since the window starts 2026-09-01.

Falls and near-falls since last review: count, circumstances, injuries, and whether any fall-risk assessment or intervention was documented. Age 71 and on a sedating antihistamine make this a priority check.
ED visits and hospital admissions in the window: reason, discharge plan, and any follow-up appointments that were missed or completed.

Medication reconciliation: review diphenhydrAMINE 25 mg (started 1959, still active) for sedation, confusion, urinary retention, constipation, and anticholinergic burden; ask the team whether the indication is current and whether any prescriber review is due.

Medication changes in window: confirm the start of simvastatin 10 mg (2026-02-06) is reflected in the care plan, check for muscle symptoms, adherence, and any lipid monitoring that is due; note any stops or dose changes not captured in the active list.

Chronic low back pain and chronic pain: pain scores, functional impact, any new analgesic use or opioid/NSAID exposure, and whether the topical hydrocortisone and any non-drug pain management are being used and reviewed.
Aspirin allergy (wheal reaction) and tree pollen allergy: verify allergy list accuracy and that the reaction documentation is complete; check for any new allergic reactions in the window.
Weight and BMI trend for obesity (BMI 30+): compare current weight to prior values, note direction and magnitude of change, and check whether nutrition or activity referral is in the care plan.
Blood pressure and cardiometabolic markers: recent readings, any lipid panel results since simvastatin start, glucose or A1c if available; flag values outside care-plan targets for team discussion.

Dental and oral health: loss of teeth (onset 2025-11-12) — check whether dental evaluation occurred, whether chewing or nutrition intake has changed, and whether dental referral or dentures are pending.
Function and ADLs/IADLs: changes in mobility, transfers, bathing, dressing, medication management, and meal preparation since last review; use of any assistive devices.

Cognition, mood and sleep: screen for new cognitive change or delirium-like symptoms (relevant given anticholinergic use), depression screen results, sleep quality, and any social isolation indicators.
Attendance and engagement: PACE center attendance, transportation issues, missed appointments, and participant or caregiver engagement in the care plan.
Caregiver and social situation: any change in living situation, primary caregiver availability or strain, financial or transportation barriers, and advance directive or healthcare proxy status.

Care-plan items due in or before the window: reassessments, goal reviews, and any open action items from the previous IDT meeting; summarize what changed and list questions for the team rather than recommending treatment.
